theory.overview: The instruction cycle—also called the fetch-decode-execute cycle—is the fundamental process by which a CPU executes programs. From boot-up to shutdown, the processor endlessly repeats this cycle: fetching the next instruction from memory, figuring out what it means, performing the requested operation, and preparing to do it again. This seemingly simple loop, executed billions of times per second, is the heartbeat of computation. Understanding the instruction cycle reveals how software instructions—mere patterns of bits—are transformed into the electrical signals that drive calculation, data movement, and control flow.

sections.title: Fetch: Getting the Instruction
sections.content: The CPU places the Program Counter (PC) value on the address bus and asserts a memory read signal. After memory access time (potentially many cycles with cache misses), the instruction appears on the data bus and is latched into the Instruction Register (IR). Simultaneously, the PC increments to point to the next sequential instruction. For variable-length instruction sets (like x86), the PC may increment by different amounts.

sections.title: Decode: Understanding the Instruction
sections.content: The control unit examines the instruction bits to determine: the operation (opcode), which registers to read, immediate values embedded in the instruction, and the operation format. For simple RISC instructions, decoding is straightforward. For complex CISC instructions, decoding may require reading additional bytes and consulting microcode ROM that translates the instruction into a sequence of micro-operations.

sections.title: Execute: Performing the Operation
sections.content: The decoded control signals activate datapath elements. For arithmetic instructions, the ALU performs the operation on register operands. For load/store instructions, memory addresses are calculated. For branch instructions, the target address is computed. This stage is where the actual computation or data movement occurs.

operations.arithmetic: ALU computes result from register operands

sections.title: Memory: Accessing Data
sections.content: If the instruction needs to access memory (load, store), this stage performs the access. The calculated address is placed on the address bus with appropriate read/write control signals. Data flows from memory to CPU (load) or CPU to memory (store). Instructions that don't access memory may skip or shorten this stage.

accessTypes.load: Read data from memory to register
accessTypes.store: Write data from register to memory

sections.title: Writeback: Storing Results
sections.content: The final stage writes results back to registers. For arithmetic instructions, the ALU result goes to the destination register. For load instructions, data from memory is written to the target register. Even instructions that don't seem to 'compute' often update the status register flags (zero, negative, carry, overflow) to reflect the operation's result.

sections.title: Interrupts: Breaking the Flow
sections.content: The CPU periodically checks for interrupt signals—requests from external devices or internal exceptions that need immediate attention. When an interrupt occurs, the CPU: finishes the current instruction, saves the PC and status (context), jumps to an interrupt handler, and eventually restores context to resume the interrupted program. This mechanism enables responsive I/O and operating system services.

keyConcepts.name: Program Counter (PC)
keyConcepts.description: Register holding the address of the next instruction to fetch. Also called Instruction Pointer (IP).

keyConcepts.name: Instruction Register (IR)
keyConcepts.description: Register holding the currently executing instruction during decode/execution.

keyConcepts.name: Microcode
keyConcepts.description: Layer of interpretation that translates complex instructions into simple micro-operations.
keyConcepts.use: Common in CISC processors like x86

keyConcepts.name: Interrupt Vector
keyConcepts.description: Table of addresses for interrupt handlers. Each interrupt type has a specific entry point.

complexity.singleCycle: All stages in one long clock cycle

steps.title: PC to Address Bus
steps.description: Place the Program Counter value on the memory address bus to specify which instruction to fetch.

steps.title: Fetch Instruction
steps.description: Memory responds with the instruction. Latch it into the Instruction Register.

steps.title: Increment PC
steps.description: Advance PC to the next instruction address.

steps.title: Decode Opcode
steps.description: Extract operation type and operand information from instruction bits.

steps.title: Read Operands
steps.description: Read source register values from the register file.

steps.title: Execute Operation
steps.description: ALU performs the operation on the source operands.

steps.title: Write Result
steps.description: Store the ALU result in the destination register.

practiceProblems.title: Instruction Cycle Stages
practiceProblems.description: What are the basic stages of the instruction cycle?
practiceProblems.explanation: The classic instruction cycle consists of Fetch (get instruction), Decode (interpret it), Execute (perform operation), optional Memory access, and Writeback (store result).

practiceProblems.title: PC Function
practiceProblems.description: What does the Program Counter hold?
practiceProblems.explanation: The PC always points to the next instruction to be fetched. After each fetch, it increments (or gets loaded with a branch target).

practiceProblems.title: Instruction Size
practiceProblems.description: If instructions are 4 bytes and PC is 0x1000, what is the PC after fetch?
practiceProblems.explanation: PC increments by the instruction size (4 bytes). 0x1000 + 4 = 0x1004.

practiceProblems.title: Microcode Purpose
practiceProblems.answer: Translating complex instructions to simple operations
practiceProblems.explanation: Microcode is a firmware layer that breaks complex CISC instructions into sequences of simpler micro-operations that the hardware can execute directly.

practiceProblems.title: Interrupt Handling
practiceProblems.description: What must the CPU do first when handling an interrupt?
practiceProblems.explanation: Before jumping to the interrupt handler, the CPU must save the current PC and status registers so it can resume the interrupted program later.

practiceProblems.title: Pipeline vs Single Cycle
practiceProblems.description: If a single-cycle CPU has 500ps cycle time and a 5-stage pipeline has 100ps cycle time, what's the theoretical speedup for many instructions?
practiceProblems.explanation: The pipeline can start a new instruction each cycle (100ps), while single-cycle takes 500ps per instruction. Theoretical speedup = 500/100 = 5x.

minigame.title: Cycle Sprint
minigame.description: Race through instruction cycles! Guide instructions through fetch, decode, execute, and writeback stages. Handle interrupts, manage the PC, and become the ultimate instruction cycle master!
instructions: Instructions enter from the left and must flow through all stages
Click on each stage to advance the instruction
Watch for interrupts - handle them immediately!
Keep the pipeline full for maximum throughput
Don't forget to update the PC after each instruction!

levels.name: Single Cycle
levels.description: Complete all stages for one instruction

snippets.title: Instruction Cycle Simulator
snippets.code:
class InstructionCycle:
    def __init__(self):
        self.pc = 0x1000
        self.ir = 0
        self.registers = [0] * 8
        self.memory = {}
        self.stage = 'FETCH'
        self.decoded = None
        self.alu_result = None
        self.mem_data = None
    
    def fetch(self, instruction):
        print(f'FETCH: PC=0x{self.pc:04X}, Getting instruction from memory')
        self.ir = instruction
        self.pc += 4
        self.stage = 'DECODE'
    
    def decode(self):
        print(f'DECODE: IR=0x{self.ir:08X}')
        opcode = (self.ir >> 26) & 0x3F
        rs = (self.ir >> 21) & 0x1F
        rt = (self.ir >> 16) & 0x1F
        rd = (self.ir >> 11) & 0x1F
        
        op_names = {0: 'ADD', 1: 'SUB', 2: 'LOAD', 3: 'STORE'}
        self.decoded = {
            'op': op_names.get(opcode, 'UNKNOWN'),
            'rs': rs,
            'rt': rt,
            'rd': rd,
            'src1': self.registers[rs],
            'src2': self.registers[rt]
        }
        print(f'  -> {self.decoded["op"]} R{rd}, R{rs}, R{rt}')
        self.stage = 'EXECUTE'
    
    def execute(self):
        print(f'EXECUTE: {self.decoded["op"]}')
        op = self.decoded['op']
        src1 = self.decoded['src1']
        src2 = self.decoded['src2']
        
        if op == 'ADD':
            self.alu_result = src1 + src2
        elif op == 'SUB':
            self.alu_result = src1 - src2
        elif op == 'LOAD':
            addr = src1 + src2
            self.alu_result = addr
        elif op == 'STORE':
            addr = src1 + src2
            self.alu_result = addr
        
        print(f'  -> ALU result: {self.alu_result}')
        self.stage = 'MEMORY' if op in ['LOAD', 'STORE'] else 'WRITEBACK'
    
    def memory_access(self):
        op = self.decoded['op']
        addr = self.alu_result
        
        if op == 'LOAD':
            self.mem_data = self.memory.get(addr, 0)
            print(f'MEMORY: LOAD from 0x{addr:04X} = {self.mem_data}')
        elif op == 'STORE':
            rt = self.decoded['rt']
            data = self.registers[rt]
            self.memory[addr] = data
            print(f'MEMORY: STORE 0x{addr:04X} = {data}')
        
        self.stage = 'WRITEBACK'
    
    def writeback(self):
        op = self.decoded['op']
        rd = self.decoded['rd']
        
        if op in ['ADD', 'SUB']:
            self.registers[rd] = self.alu_result
            print(f'WRITEBACK: R{rd} = {self.alu_result}')
        elif op == 'LOAD':
            self.registers[rd] = self.mem_data
            print(f'WRITEBACK: R{rd} = {self.mem_data} (loaded)')
        
        self.stage = 'FETCH'
    
    def run_instruction(self, instr):
        self.fetch(instr)
        self.decode()
        self.execute()
        if self.stage == 'MEMORY':
            self.memory_access()
        self.writeback()
        print('---')

# Test: ADD R1, R2, R3 (R1 = R2 + R3)
cycle = InstructionCycle()
cycle.registers[2] = 10
cycle.registers[3] = 20

# Encode: ADD=0, R2=2, R3=3, R1=1
instr = (0 << 26) | (2 << 21) | (3 << 16) | (1 << 11)
cycle.run_instruction(instr)

print(f'Registers after: {cycle.registers[1:4]}')  # R1=30, R2=10, R3=20
